rules.statement: Limit failed password attempts per account (keyed by the account's user name), not per remote address or client, on every path that verifies a password: interactive sign-in, the password grant and self-service password change.
rules.why: A request rate limiter that counts per address or per client doesn't stop a guesser that spreads attempts across addresses. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.2.2 requires a per-account limit.
rules.check: Look for a new or changed password-verification path that doesn't consult the per-account attempt limiter, or a counter key that includes the remote address.

rules.statement: When a password is refused because the attempt limit is reached, give exactly the same response as for a wrong password, and do the same work by verifying the submitted password against the dummy hash, never against the stored hash.
rules.why: A refusal that returns a different answer, skips hashing, or verifies the stored hash (which can change the verification count or trigger a rehash) reveals through the response or its timing that the limit was reached or that the password was right.
rules.check: In refusal branches, look for a distinct error code or message, an early return that skips hashing, or a verification against the account's stored hash.

rules.statement: Count every password verification that doesn't succeed, including refusals at the limit and user names that no account has (counted under the name as submitted), and count it only after the verification, never before.
rules.why: Counting unknown names and refusals the same way as wrong passwords keeps the limit from revealing whether an account exists. Counting before verification would also count successes and lock out legitimate users.
rules.check: Look for failure-recording code that skips unknown accounts or refusals, or that increments the counter before the password is verified.

rules.statement: Record a failed authentication attempt with CancellationToken.None rather than the request's token.
rules.why: A client that disconnects right after submitting a guess must not be able to skip the count.
rules.check: Find calls that record failed attempts and check whether they pass the request/HttpContext cancellation token.

rules.statement: Clear an account's failed-attempt count after a successful password verification and after an administrator sets or resets the password.
rules.why: Failures that come before a successful authentication should be disregarded (NIST), and an administrator's reset should restore access for the end user whose password was being guessed.
rules.check: Look for success paths and admin password create/reset paths that don't reset the attempt counter.

rules.statement: Make a security-control limiter fail closed: let an exception from its backing counter store propagate so authentication fails, rather than catching it and allowing the attempt.
rules.why: An outage of the shared state must not lift a security control. Only capacity-protecting rate limiters may fail open.
rules.check: In a security limiter, look for try/catch around counter-store calls that swallows the exception or returns 'not limited'.

rules.statement: Key shared-state entries for user names by a digest of the folded name, not by the name itself, and never log the user name when an attempt limit refuses a password.
rules.why: Shared state and logs must hold no user names. An operator should see the refusal (with the tenant and the limit) without the name being disclosed.
rules.check: Look for counter keys built from the raw user name, and for log calls on the limit/refusal path that include the user name.

rules.statement: Don't add a database lookup that runs only when an account exists, or a separate pre-lookup to resolve the account's name, before password verification. Find the account and its hash with a single lookup.
rules.why: A query that runs only for existing accounts adds time that no hash hides, which reveals whether the account exists. A second lookup also lets the counted account differ from the verified one.
rules.check: In credential-verification code, look for extra queries or claim reads that depend on whether the account was found, or a second find-by-name call before verification.

rules.statement: Merge security-limit settings across scopes so that a narrower scope can only tighten them: an attempt limit merges with Min and a lockout window merges with Max, each validated against a bounded range.
rules.why: A narrower scope (such as a tenant) must not loosen a security control set at a broader scope, and the limit must stay within NIST's maximum of 100.
rules.check: Look for new security-limit settings that merge with replace semantics or in the loosening direction, or that have no range validation.
